item.title: A tuned topographic map hierarchy formats visual working memory load
item.description:
Relevance: 36% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Harvey, B. M., van Ackooij, M., van Helden, J. F. L., Hendrikx, E., van der Stoep, N., Gayet, S. M., Paul, J. M.
Visual working memory tasks rely on neural systems that scale activity with task load. Traditional models assume higher demands are met by monotonically increasing activity within a single process, implying high informational redundancy across responses. However, theories of cognitive control suggest processing strategies change with task demands, flexibly linking sensory inputs to behavior. Using 7T fMRI and neural encoding models, we hypothesized and confirmed that association cortices format task load-dependent responses using sensory-like neural tuning. We identified populations selectively tuned to specific loads, forming 11 topographic maps per hemisphere hierarchically organized from posterior sensory to anterior executive regions across a fronto-parieto-occipital network. Tuning persisted across performance and trial-order controls, was absent without memory task demands, and predicted behavioral accuracy after load changes. These findings demonstrate that human association cortices distribute task demands using continuously varying processing pathways, adapting sensory-like tuning to decorrelate responses and reduce information redundency during cognitive control.

item.title: Neuronal communication subspaces arise across prefrontal-striatal circuits prior to gaze-directed object selection and develop with learning
item.description:
Relevance: 36% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Poggi, P. G., Hassani, S.-A., Neumann, A., Brust, D., Boroujeni, K. B., Tiesinga, P., Womelsdorf, T.
How neuronal ensembles determine the most relevant object to attend to remains unresolved but likely involves coordinating information across multiple brain areas. We found support for this hypothesis in latent firing co-variations across the prefrontal cortex (PFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and head of the caudate (CD) during and after attention-set learning. Before gaze shifted to an object, neuronal communication subspaces emerged across area pairs. While exploring options during learning, ACC and PFC led communication over the CD prior to gaze shifts, which switched to the CD and PFC leading the ACC when exploiting learned attention sets. Neurons participating in exploration- and exploitation-specific subspaces were partly segregated and carried information about the value and location of the to-be-selected objects, suggesting they guide attention and gaze.

item.title: Self-generated action shapes theta phase alignment at encoding and later recollection
item.description:
Relevance: 34% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Chen, Q., Sui, J.
Across species, self-directed action is linked to theta rhythms and better memory, but such action combines choosing, moving, and controlling the outcome. Whether choosing and control over the outcome shape recollection, and the encoding dynamics that support it, remains unclear. Three preregistered experiments in human participants separated these components while holding movement constant. Participants encoded scene pairs by dragging either a freely chosen scene or one indicated by the program, with fluent or disrupted feedback. Recognition was tested after 24 hours (and immediately in Experiment 2), using Remember/Know judgments. Experiment 3 recorded scalp electroencephalography during encoding. Choosing improved recognition, more for recollection than familiarity. A smaller benefit extended to the unselected scene, although less consistently after latency adjustment. Disrupted feedback lowered rated agency but did not reduce memory at 24 hours. In Experiment 2, however, recollection declined less over 24 hours after self-generated than externally generated action, but only under fluent feedback. Choosing increased action-onset-locked theta and alpha phase alignment (inter-trial phase coherence), whereas disrupted feedback reduced alignment later. The selection effects survived matching for response-initiation-latency. Trial by trial, later posterior theta alignment (353-570 ms) predicted Remember over Know responses, whereas early frontal alpha alignment (127-245 ms) predicted Remember over Forgotten responses. These findings link self-generated action to the timing of encoding-related oscillations and to subsequent recollection. The association between later posterior theta alignment and Remember-Know discrimination is consistent with a role for theta phase coordination in associative binding.

item.title: Sampling the Training Trajectory of Vision Models Reveals a Mismatch with Human Visual Development
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Proietti, M., Bersch, D., Schaumlöffel, T., Cerdas, D. G., Franaszek-Traczewska, A., Zwad, H. E., Xie, S., Baldauf, M., Sylvester, T., Schätz, C. M., Höhl, S., Köster, M., Cichy, R. M., Roig, G.
We compare time-resolved EEG representational geometry across seven age groups, from 6 months to adulthood, with representations sampled throughout training from supervised and self-supervised ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16. Previous model-brain comparisons mostly used adult brain recordings and untrained or fully trained networks. We find that successive training stages do not systematically progress from child- to adult-like neural representations: alignment with every age group from 4 years onward emerges early in training and remains stable. Training adds substantial alignment beyond the untrained architecture, similarly at every age. Finally, categorical structure and spatial frequency each explain a stable share of the neural geometry at every age, with apparent age-related increases in categorical organization reflecting increased EEG reliability. Because standard training on full-resolution images aligns with all ages early, and spatial frequency, which depends on maturing visual acuity, strongly shapes the neural geometry, developmentally structured visual input may help models follow human visual development.

item.title: Learning from Natural Images Untangles Number Sense
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Yechan Cho, Hyeonsu Lee, Emma Deneuville, Jaeson Jang
arXiv:2611.33615v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Numerical cognition is a simple yet fundamental ability that remains challenging for modern vision-language models. Meanwhile, number sense is already present in numerically na\"ive animals, suggesting that it can emerge without explicit numerical learning. Deep neural networks provide a related observation, with numerosity-selective units appearing after training on unrelated natural-image tasks and even before any training. However, these findings leave unresolved whether visual learning contributes beyond the spontaneous emergence of numerical selectivity. Human development provides a clue, as children become better at making judgments in which numerosity and proportion conflict. Here, we introduce a geometric framework to trace how representations of these two quantities change across learning. Although untrained and pretrained networks exhibited similar unit-level numerosity selectivity and basic comparison performance, natural-image pretraining increased the angle between numerosity and proportion subspaces while reducing their overlap, supporting more robust readout under conflict. Direct manipulation of these geometric properties further demonstrated their functional contributions to decoding accuracy and functional independence. Importantly, conventional supervised pretraining was not essential for quantity separation, which also emerged through self-supervised learning without category labels and synthetic-image training without natural-image exposure. Together, our findings suggest that structured visual learning can refine spontaneously emerging number sense into robust and functionally independent quantity representations without explicit numerical training.

item.title: Prioritization over certainty: Action planning in visual working memory iscoupled with selective attention, rather than action predictability
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Özdemir, S., Ataseven, N., Kruijne, W., Akyürek, E. G., Schneider, D.
When visual information is no longer perceptually available, working memory (WM) allows us to act on sensory representations. But does this guidance require attentional prioritization? We addressed this question by asking participants to remember two oriented bars that were later tested with one predictable and one random probe. This design allowed us to track when a remembered orientation became linked to a specific response hand and whether that link depended on which item was currently prioritized in WM. Response preparation followed prioritization: even when the later response was predictable, no motor preparation emerged while the corresponding item remained latent. Our exploratory analyses showed that prospective action information reduced the need to reprioritize latent items, and that learned stimulus-response mappings generalized across task contexts, suggesting that task-relevant features of visual WM can be partly offloaded onto motor codes. These findings show that active response preparation is coupled with selective attention, while motor representations can also support maintenance in a visual WM task.

item.title: Learning sequences where conflicting events predict upcoming stimuli
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: SocArXiv
Luc Vermeylen et al.
"Limited evidence for predicting from conflict: A reverse cueing study reveals the limits of congruency-stimulus learning". Jiménez, Abrahamse, Méndez and Braem (2020) showed that participants can learn to use sequential color-color contingencies in a Stroop-task in order to respond faster and more accurately, but they failed to find the same learning pattern with sequential color-congruency contingencies, thus suggesting that people are unable to reliably learn these contingencies. In the current pre-registered study, we will try to further explore sequential control-response associations: we will attempt to test whether the previous Jiménez, et al. (2020) null-finding was due to people’s inability to learn links between stimuli and control demands across trials, or prepare for next trial’s congruency conditions . Hence, we will employ a Stroop task where congruency levels predict the color of the next trial (thus, the opposite of Jiménez, et al., 2020, where colors predicted congruency levels). This series of experiments will allow us to understand whether people are completely incapable to learn contingencies between stimuli and control demands across trials, or, instead, whether they struggle to prepare for congruency conditions, but can use the congruency level of a previous stimulus to gain an advantage in the next one.

item.title: Whether untrained networks beat trained ones at V1 depends on a normalisation convention: evidence from two fMRI datasets
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Nils Leutenegger
arXiv:2611.15533v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Untrained convolutional networks have been reported to rival or beat trained networks as models of primary visual cortex (V1), and we had reported such an advantage in THINGS fMRI. Under a pre-specified ridge readout, the trained network was ahead at every pooling grid in THINGS and in NSD (8 of 8 subjects), also when voxel responses were centred within runs. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) in THINGS depended on analysis choices (28 analyses: intervals above 0 in 5, below 0 in 9, including 0 in 14); in NSD with its standard normalisation, none of 28 analyses favoured the untrained network. The untrained advantage appears when a response profile common to all trials is left in the voxel patterns and model units are not centred, under correlation distance: removing the session-mean profile in THINGS reduced it from +0.030 to +0.005; with raw betas it reached +0.100 in THINGS, appeared in the THINGS test images, and appeared in NSD (+0.116, 8 of 8 subjects, a pre-specified prediction), where it was confined to this one of 28 analyses. With the profile left in, both representational dissimilarity matrices are dominated by per-image response amplitude, which in V1 tracks contrast energy, and the untrained network's matrix is more amplitude-dominated; the amplitude itself is matched equally by both networks; removing the amplitude structure from both matrices removes the advantage in NSD (+0.116 to -0.009, 8 of 8 subjects). A luminance-and-contrast baseline outperformed every network under ridge in both datasets (point estimates); the networks reached 10-15% of the NSD noise-ceiling lower bound. 24 of 88 pre-specified predictions were not met. We recommend centring or normalising voxel responses within session, reporting the sensitivity of RSA rankings to this choice and to model-unit centring, and replicating on a second dataset.

item.title: A Geometric View for Understanding Concept Learning and Neuron Interpretation in Sparse Autoencoders
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Chenhao Zhang, Chris Lin, Xiaojian Chen, Hanqi Feng, Su-In Lee
arXiv:2606.07007v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a unified mathematical framework for a geometric understanding of concept learning and neuron interpretation in sparse autoencoders (SAEs). While SAEs improve interpretability of neural networks by learning sparse feature representations, a principled definition of ''concept'' and ''learning'' remains unclear. We formalize concepts as sets of data points and cast concept learning as a set-alignment problem between human-defined and model-induced concepts. This formulation distinguishes three increasingly strong notions of learning -- detection, separation, and approximation -- and yields geometric conditions, error bounds, and capacity constraints for when concepts can be represented by individual neurons or multi-neuron units. It also provides a set-theoretic account for common SAE phenomena, including feature splitting, feature absorption, feature families, and hierarchical concepts. Finally, we connect concept learning and neuron interpretation through formal concept analysis, showing that the two directions need not agree and that their many-to-many structure can be organized by concept lattices. Experiments on synthetic data with ReLU and Top-$K$ SAEs illustrate the theory and reveal the effects of SAE size and sparsity on concept learning.

item.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Cognitive Complexity in LLMs via Linear Probing using Bloom's Taxonomy
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Bianca Raimondi, Maurizio Gabbrielli
arXiv:2602.17229v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The black-box nature of Large Language Models necessitates novel evaluation frameworks that transcend surface-level performance metrics. This study investigates the internal neural representations of the levels of complexity using Bloom's Taxonomy as a hierarchical lens. By analyzing high-dimensional activation vectors from different LLMs, we probe whether different Bloom levels, ranging from basic recall (Remember) to abstract synthesis (Create), are linearly separable within the model's residual streams. Our results demonstrate that linear classifiers achieve high accuracy across all Bloom levels, providing evidence that level information is encoded in a linearly accessible subspace of the model's representations. These findings provide evidence that the model organizes representations according to Bloom categories early in the forward pass, with representations becoming increasingly separable across layers.

item.title: A Graph Signal Processing Perspective on Numerical Sequence Representations in LLM In-Context Learning
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Jiajun Bao, Zihao Qi, Toni J. B. Liu, Gurbir Arora, Rapha\"el Sarfati, Nicolas Boull\'e, Christopher J. Earls
arXiv:2608.03015v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pretrained large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated in-context learning (ICL) capabilities for numerical inference over sequences serialized as text. Prior work has identified and characterized this form of numerical inference primarily through output-level evaluations such as prediction error. However, how numerical information is organized within LLM representations remains much less understood. To study this internal organization, we adopt a graph signal processing perspective in which attention induces a weighted graph over tokens, while token hidden states define signals on its nodes. Quantitative graph-spectral diagnostics and qualitative token-graph visualizations reveal that representations become more clearly differentiated by input dynamical complexity as context length increases. Simpler inputs produce attention-induced token graphs with stronger global connectivity and smoother, spectrally concentrated hidden-state signals, whereas more complex inputs produce more localized graphs and hidden-state signals with broader spectral support and greater high-frequency energy. These diagnostics and visualizations offer an interpretable view of the internal structure associated with numerical ICL, beyond what output-level prediction error alone reveals. Together, these findings point to systematic, context-dependent internal signatures associated with numerical ICL that are qualitatively conserved across model families.

item.title: Disciplined Anthropomorphism: How to Extend Cognitive Language to Artificial Intelligence
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Matthieu Queloz
arXiv:2611.34090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Researchers increasingly describe AI in cognitive terms such as "understanding" and "believing", while critics denounce this as wishful anthropomorphism. Both sides align in taking a subsumptive approach, however: they ask whether AI systems fall under concepts minted for human beings, reporting verdicts as discoveries about those systems when they are largely determined by conceptual frames. Yet the problem AI poses is precisely the problem of how to conceptually frame these systems, and the explosive rise of anthropomorphism is best seen as a response to this problem that needs disciplining rather than discouragement. A disciplined anthropomorphism, I argue, should disentangle the inferential connections bundled up in our cognitive concepts and ask which connections to preserve, sever, or forge for AI. The disciplining then comes, on the one hand, from the human conceptual needs that give point to the drawing of these connections and motivate the concepts' extension in the first place; and, on the other hand, from empirical and especially mechanistic evidence that supports and constrains these connections. By reverse-engineering a concept's point in relation to a particular need before re-engineering it to better serve that point in our dealings with AI, anthropomorphizing extensions can be point-based, transposing the work those concepts do for us while revising the inferential workings through which they do it. Transposing human-tailored conceptions of understanding and belief on the pivot of the underlying conceptual needs gives us just the definitional freedom required to accommodate how AI systems differ from us, yielding conceptions that are not just thinned-out versions of existing ones, but potentially richer and better fitted to the peculiarities of AI.

item.title: Learning World Models through Contrastive Identification of Actions
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv AI
Hayeong Lee, Youngjun Suh, Byung-Jun Lee
arXiv:2611.32776v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Latent world models enable goal-directed planning from offline visual data, but prediction alone does not specify which action-related distinctions their representations should preserve. Inverse dynamics provides auxiliary supervision, yet squared-error action regression rewards additional information only through changes in the conditional action mean. We propose Contrastive Identification of Actions (CIA), which identifies the executed action among alternatives sampled from a history-conditioned behavior proposal. Comparing actions plausible in the same context targets information supplied by the next latent beyond history. Under exact behavior matching, we show that CIA can reward action information that leaves optimal inverse-regression error unchanged, and verify this distinction through a controlled learning example. CIA achieves higher planner-averaged mean success than the base world model and a regression inverse-dynamics baseline across five visual control benchmarks, without modifying the planner.

item.title: Can image generation help visual reasoning? An empirical study
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Xueyang Yu, Yifan Jing, Taiming Lu, Linrong Cai, Zhipeng Cai, Yunyang Xiong, Gabriel Sarch, Zhuang Liu
arXiv:2611.34935v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language models think in words; then multimodal models might think in images. We test whether a generated helper improves the answer to a visual question. A model describes the helper it needs and then answers using the original and generated images together. Across 13 vision-language model and generator pairs, generation lowers mean accuracy by 3.7 percentage points, with declines on nine of ten tasks. Two unified models, BAGEL and Janus-Pro-7B, each lose accuracy on eight tasks. On VSTAR, adding a generated image to the same planning hint lowers accuracy by 10.47 points. Repeated image edits yield different outcomes across tasks. ChartQAPro and MathVista stay below their no-generation baselines, while ERQA gains three points after ten edits.

item.title: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis in Jacobian-Space: Language and Vision Models Agree Approximately Up to a Rotation
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Ross Murphy, Gabriel Brostow
arXiv:2611.33304v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) posits that AI models converge toward a shared representation of the world, even when trained on different data modalities. Previous work has found evidence for the PRH in the activations of vision and language models. In this work, we ask whether vision and language models also converge in how they act on these representations: precisely, in how these internal representations affect the models' output. At a chosen layer of a transformer, the Jacobian lens gives every word in the vocabulary (or class in an image classifier) a vector in the hidden state: the vector that most increases the model's tendency to generate that word, at that position or later, or to predict that class. Collectively, these vectors make up what is referred to as the model's J-space. We find evidence of the PRH in J-space across vision and language models, and furthermore, we find that J-spaces mostly converge up to a rotation. That is, a single rotation, fitted on a subset of words, approximately maps one model's J-space onto another's, and so applies to words and classes it was not fitted on. A word's vector, rotated from a text-only language model's J-space into the visual patch tokens of a vision-language model, changes the object the vision-language model says is in the image (and only in the image region where it is added). Rotated into an image generator's text conditioning, a word's vector changes the object in the generated image. Rotated into an ImageNet classifier (trained without text), it raises that object's class score above almost all others, and vice versa. This suggests that models converge not only in how they represent the world, but also in how they act on it.

item.title: Decoupling the clocks of learning and computing in spiking neural networks
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Michalis Pagkalos, Panayiota Poirazi
arXiv:2611.34381v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Biological intelligence thrives on minimal power despite its noisy, imperfect components, with neurons that communicate through voltage spikes. Brain-inspired computing seeks to bring such efficiency to real devices, which requires training methods tailored to them. The standard way to train spiking neural networks, backpropagation through time, computes weight updates through every step of a simulated device, so faithful or long simulations can make training costly and unstable. Here we show that spiking networks can learn reliably and efficiently by decoupling the clock of learning from that of computing. Our method, ChronoProp, calculates weight updates from each neuron's spike counts in fixed time bins using its measured input-output function. Compared with backpropagation through time, ChronoProp reaches similar accuracy in image classification, with about 3 times less training time and 20 times less memory at the finest timestep tested, and up to 10 times fewer spikes. On spoken-word benchmarks, ChronoProp is far more accurate in recurrent networks at fine timesteps, and with simple, hardware-compatible techniques it approaches the best published models. These networks also tolerate simulated hardware defects and limitations better than those trained with backpropagation through time. Therefore, ChronoProp enables stable and efficient training in simulations close to the continuous time of analog hardware.

item.title: Two Timescales of Forgetting in Fine-tuning of Language Models: Fast Behavioral Suppression and Slow Representational Drift
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Yilin Luo, Jin Hwa Lee, Andrew M. Saxe, Antonio Sclocchi
arXiv:2611.33302v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Today, a core pipeline of artificial intelligence systems is pretraining on a broad range of text corpora and then fine-tuning on specific tasks or desired behaviors. Yet we still have limited understanding of how fine-tuning on a restricted data distribution modifies representations acquired during pretraining. In particular, it remains unclear whether surface behavioral suppression happens together with the erasure of latent representations that support it. In this work, we study supervised fine-tuning (SFT) by pretraining transformers on a controlled context-free grammar with hierarchical latent structure, the Random Hierarchy Model (RHM), and fine-tuning with a restricted subset of its generative rules. While during pretraining the model's ability to generate with the correct grammar rules coincides with building the internal representations of the corresponding latent, we find that SFT exhibits a very different dynamics: (i) the generation of deleted rules changes on a fast timescale inversely proportional to the magnitude of the token-latent correlation; meanwhile, their corresponding representations stay intact; (ii) the hidden representations of the deleted rules become forgotten on a much longer timescale, associated with a slow drift of the network parameters. Finally, we observe analogous results in a realistic setup with natural language, suggesting that this timescale separation in forgetting is a more general phenomenon of fine-tuning language models.

item.title: EEG-World: Context-Conditioned Dynamics of the Watching Brain
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Junxiang Zhang, Jiayu Zuo, Wenhao Ye, Junfeng Xia, Xiang Chen, Mo Wang, Quanying Liu
arXiv:2611.32825v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Brain encoding models predict neural responses from audiovisual input, but typically overlook how ongoing brain activity shapes an individual's response. We introduce EEG-World, a recurrent world model that forecasts 10 seconds of EEG band-power dynamics from 6 seconds of preceding EEG and the subsequent audiovisual stimulus. Pretrained on continuous EEG, EEG-World learns shared neural dynamics and adapts to unseen individuals through lightweight subject-specific readouts. Using 2,584 hours of EEG from 78 participants, we show that nonlinear recurrent forecasting surpasses strong history-aware linear baselines at scale. EEG-World achieves a forecasting correlation of 0.261 versus 0.233 for the strongest history-and-video linear model, with a 3.3-second forecasting-horizon advantage. Its learned dynamics transfer to unseen participants, outperforming the linear baseline in 23 of 24 individuals after calibration. While ongoing EEG history accounts for most predictive performance, controlled stimulus analyses reveal an additional video-dependent component. This component also enables evaluation of visual representations, with V-JEPA 2 improving clip-locked prediction by 35% over combined CLIP and DINOv2 features. Our results demonstrate the value of transferable neural dynamics for individual EEG forecasting and highlight the importance of separating state-driven from stimulus-driven predictability.

item.title: The Marauder's Map: B\'{e}zier Manifolds Reveal Hidden Surfaces for Model Merging and Ensembling
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Abhiram Iyer, Mark T. Harnett, Sarthak Chandra
arXiv:2611.33353v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Neural circuits are famously more robust than deep networks. This is often explained through degeneracy, where structurally distinct configurations support the same function. However, real biological systems exhibit a more flexible form of degeneracy in which specialized circuits continually adapt towards new competencies through localized changes while preserving existing function. Deep learning studies degeneracy through mode connectivity, which connects same-task networks by low-loss curves, sheets, or volumes. However, the field lacks a counterpart to flexible degeneracy, which demands more than ordinary mode connectivity. Defining such an analogue requires asking whether many independently initialized models trained on distinct tasks can be connected by a high-dimensional region of multi-task solutions. We introduce $\textit{Nimbus}$, which learns a high-dimensional B\'ezier manifold connecting $N$ specialists, going beyond the one-dimensional paths and two-dimensional sheets of mode connectivity work. A naive parameterization would scale combinatorially with $N$, but $\textit{Nimbus}$ requires learning corrections of only 3 interaction orders, showing that the connecting manifold has surprisingly low complexity yet supports multi-task competencies. The resulting manifold forms a navigable "Marauder's Map" that connects specialist models through a shared geometry of competent solutions. Trained across vision and language domains, $\textit{Nimbus}$ produces manifolds that are functionally and locally weight-flat: ensembles sampled from them degrade more gracefully than baselines under input and weight perturbations, with the largest gains in NLL loss and calibration error. $\textit{Nimbus}$ supplies a deep learning interpretation of flexible degeneracy, recasting model connectivity from a low-dimensional path between distant solutions into a high-dimensional volume of nearby ones.

item.title: Error correction necessitates immediate, answer-containing feedback: Challenging error suppression, episodic reinstatement, and semantic mediation accounts
item.description:
Relevance: 22% | Source: SocArXiv
Matthew Rhodes et al.
Generating errors during learning benefits subsequent recall, particularly when corrective feedback is presented immediately. Feedback in existing research conflates notification of error commission with provision of the correct target. Across two experiments, we examined the effects of immediate feedback, delayed feedback, and delayed feedback with an immediate “error” warning on cued and error-cued recall. In Experiment 1, warnings did not mitigate the detrimental effect of delayed feedback on cued recall, indicating that optimal pretesting requires immediate, answer-containing feedback. This challenges two hypotheses of errorful learning: that suppressing errors at encoding facilitates error correction (the error-suppression hypothesis), and that error commission promotes context binding which enables episodic reinstatement during feedback and at test (episodic reinstatement hypothesis). Immediate feedback improved cued recall performance but not participants’ ability to recall the accuracy of their initial responses, further contradicting the possibility of episodic reinstatement at test facilitating target recovery. In Experiment 2, delaying feedback improved error-cued recall, undermining mediator-based accounts which assume that errors function as additional retrieval cues, increasing the likelihood of successfully retrieving the target. We propose that error commission increases attention to the target at encoding, strengthening the cue–target retrieval route.
